question: Which product category brings in the most revenue, and how much?

golden.rubric: Correct if it names Outerwear as the top category and gives its revenue as about $464,861 (accept $464,000-$465,700, or a figure rounded to $465k). Wrong if it names another category, or a revenue off by more than $1,000.

verification.primaryAxis: group by category across all lines, rank by summed sale_price
verification.variesAxis: no grouping: filter to Outerwear alone and sum, which cannot inherit a mis-grouping
verification.note: Ranked group-by and the single filtered sum agree to the cent.

golden.canonicalQuery: run: t_order_items extend { join_one: t_products on product_id = t_products.product_id } -> { group_by: category is t_products.category; aggregate: revenue is sale_price.sum(); order_by: revenue desc; limit: 1 }

question: Which brand sells at the highest margin rate?

golden.rubric: Correct if it names Harbor, with a margin rate of about 50.2% (accept 49.7-50.7, or 0.502 as a fraction). Wrong if it names another brand. A margin rate computed per line and averaged, rather than as total margin over total revenue, lands near the same figure for this data and is acceptable so long as the brand is Harbor and the rate is stated.

verification.primaryAxis: group by brand, ratio of summed margin to summed revenue
verification.variesAxis: no grouping: filter to Harbor alone and take the same ratio, so a mis-grouped denominator cannot survive
verification.note: Harbor is the only brand above 50%; the next is Loft at 48.4%, so the ranking is not close enough to turn on rounding.

golden.canonicalQuery: run: t_order_items extend { join_one: t_products on product_id = t_products.product_id } extend { dimension: line_margin is sale_price - t_products.cost, line_markdown is t_products.retail_price - sale_price } -> { group_by: brand is t_products.brand; aggregate: margin_rate is line_margin.sum() / sale_price.sum(); order_by: margin_rate desc; limit: 1 }

question: Which month of 2025 had the highest revenue?

golden.rubric: Correct if it names December 2025, with revenue about $125,924 (accept $125,400-$126,500, or 'about $126k'). Wrong if it names another month. Naming the month without a figure is acceptable: the question asks which month.

verification.primaryAxis: group by month within 2025, rank by summed sale_price
verification.variesAxis: no grouping: filter to December 2025 alone and sum
verification.note: December leads November by $14,931, well clear of any rounding.

golden.canonicalQuery: run: t_order_items -> { where: created_at.year = @2025; group_by: order_month is created_at.month; aggregate: revenue is sale_price.sum(); order_by: revenue desc; limit: 1 }

question: How many orders does the average customer place?

golden.rubric: Correct if it gives about 11.3 orders per customer (accept 11.0-11.6). Wrong if it gives the line-item count per customer (about 26), or the raw order count. A stated basis of 'customers who have ordered' (974) rather than all customers on file (1,000) is the correct reading, since the fact table only knows the former.

verification.primaryAxis: distinct orders divided by distinct ordering customers, no grouping
verification.variesAxis: group by customer first, then average the per-customer order counts -- a different shape that also exposes a customer with no orders
verification.note: 11,000 orders over 974 ordering customers. The two derivations agree because every customer in the fact table has at least one order; 26 customers on file have none and are correctly outside the denominator.

golden.canonicalQuery: run: t_order_items -> { aggregate: orders_per_customer is count(order_id) / count(customer_id) }

question: Who is our single biggest customer by total spend?

golden.rubric: Correct if it names Delilah Okafor (customer_id 884) with about $8,818 of spend (accept $8,750-$8,900). WRONG if it names Mila Costa with about $17,988: that is three different customers who share a name, collapsed by grouping on full_name instead of customer_id. Naming the customer id, or the name with the id, is ideal; the name alone is acceptable only if it is Delilah Okafor.

verification.primaryAxis: group by customer_id, rank by summed sale_price
verification.variesAxis: no grouping: filter to customer_id 884 alone and sum, and separately count how many customers share each name
verification.note: 1,000 customers hold only 769 distinct names. Grouping by name alone promotes three Mila Costas (ids 84, 230, 326) to a false top spender of $17,988. The model's own top_customers view groups by name AND customer_id, so the right route exists.

golden.canonicalQuery: run: t_order_items -> { group_by: customer_id; aggregate: spend is sale_price.sum(); order_by: spend desc; limit: 1 }

question: What were net sales in 2025, excluding cancelled and returned items?

golden.rubric: Correct if it gives about $834,216 (accept $833,000-$835,500). WRONG if it gives about $912,857: that is gross sales, which is what the model's total_sales measure returns, because total_sales carries no status filter. An answer that reports gross while stating plainly that it could not exclude cancelled and returned items is a near match, not a match.

verification.primaryAxis: sum sale_price over 2025 excluding status Cancelled and Returned
verification.variesAxis: subtract the other way: gross 2025 sales minus the summed Cancelled and Returned lines
verification.note: Gross $912,857.17 less $78,641.55 of cancelled and returned lines gives $834,215.62 -- an 8.6% gap, far too large for a judge to read a gross answer as correct. The model defines no net measure.

golden.canonicalQuery: run: t_order_items -> { where: created_at.year = @2025 and status != 'Cancelled' and status != 'Returned'; aggregate: net_sales is sale_price.sum() }

question: How much revenue came from customers who signed up in 2025?

golden.rubric: Correct if it gives about $488,971 (accept $487,500-$490,500). The model defines no cohort measure, but customers.signup_date IS exposed as a dimension and the customers join is declared, so the answer is reachable by filtering on it -- this case tests whether the agent builds the two-step route, not whether the model has the concept. An answer that says it cannot be determined is a no match, because the route exists.

verification.primaryAxis: join customers, filter on signup_date year, sum sale_price
verification.variesAxis: two steps instead of one: collect the 2025-signup customer ids first, then filter the fact table to that id set
verification.note: 247 of the 253 customers who signed up in 2025 placed an order; the other six are correctly absent from a revenue figure. Both routes give $488,970.54.

golden.canonicalQuery: run: t_order_items extend { join_one: t_customers on customer_id = t_customers.customer_id } -> { where: t_customers.signup_date.year = @2025; aggregate: cohort_revenue is sale_price.sum() }

question: On average, how far below list price do we actually sell?

golden.rubric: Correct if it gives a discount of about 5.4% off list (accept 5.0-5.9%, stated either as a percentage or as selling at about 94.6% of list). The model names no discount measure, but products.retail_price is exposed as a dimension, so the answer is reachable. Note the grain trap: retail_price belongs to the product, so summing it directly is a symmetric aggregate over distinct products and gives a nonsense denominator -- the correct route is a per-line expression. Both the line-weighted figure (5.43%) and the unweighted per-line average (5.41%) are acceptable.

verification.primaryAxis: one minus summed sale_price over summed retail_price, weighted by line
verification.variesAxis: unweighted instead: average the per-line discount fraction, which weights a cheap line the same as an expensive one
verification.note: Weighted 5.43% and unweighted 5.41% agree to within 0.02 points, so the rubric does not have to choose between them.

golden.canonicalQuery: run: t_order_items extend { join_one: t_products on product_id = t_products.product_id } extend { dimension: line_margin is sale_price - t_products.cost, line_markdown is t_products.retail_price - sale_price } -> { aggregate: discount_off_list is line_markdown.sum() / (line_markdown.sum() + sale_price.sum()) }

question: Which sales region brings in the most revenue?

golden.rubric: Correct if it names the South, with revenue about $781,182 (accept $779,000-$783,500, or 'about $781k'). Wrong if it names another region. This one reaches the regions lookup through customers.state, two joins from the fact table.

verification.primaryAxis: join customers then regions on state, group by region, rank
verification.variesAxis: no grouping: filter to the South's states and sum, which does not depend on the group-by resolving the two-hop join
verification.note: The South leads the West by $292,464. Every one of the 50 states in customers resolves to a region, so no revenue falls outside the rollup.

golden.canonicalQuery: run: t_order_items extend { join_one: t_customers on customer_id = t_customers.customer_id } extend { join_one: t_regions on t_customers.state = t_regions.state } -> { group_by: region is t_regions.region; aggregate: revenue is sale_price.sum(); order_by: revenue desc; limit: 1 }

golden.rubric: This question has no single defensible answer and is here to see what the agent does with one. Match if the answer states which definition of 'best' it used -- total spend, order count, or gross margin -- and the customers it names are correct under that definition, identified by customer_id or by a name that is unique on file. Near match if it gives a defensible ranking but never says what 'best' means. No match if it groups customers by full_name alone, which merges distinct people who share a name, or if it names customers that are top under no definition. Asking the user which definition they want, instead of answering, is a match: the question is genuinely underspecified.
golden.mustState: which definition of 'best' it used, and customers correct under that definition

verification.primaryAxis: not applicable: a criteria golden holds no value
verification.note: By spend the top is Delilah Okafor (884, $8,818); by order count it is Amelia Cohen (80 orders). The two rankings disagree, which is the point of the case.

question: What were our summer sales in 2025?
source: as-received/questions.md (hand-authored question list, 2026-09-21); the summer window is a business convention stated in that file's conventions section

golden.rubric: The company's sales calendar defines summer as 25 May to 15 September inclusive (as-received/questions.md). Correct if it gives about $267,423 for that window (accept $266,000-$268,800). WRONG if it gives about $213,939, which is the meteorological June-August reading, or any other window's figure reported as though it were summer. A near match if it states the window it used plainly -- 'summer, taken as June to August, was $213,939' -- because the answer is then checkable and only the convention is missing. Asking which window the business means is a match. Nothing in storefront.malloy expresses a season, so no route through the model supplies this.

verification.primaryAxis: filter the window directly and sum
verification.variesAxis: the complement: all of 2025 less every line outside the window, which shares no boundary arithmetic with the first
verification.note: Window $267,422.53 and complement $267,422.53 agree to the cent. A June-August reading gives $213,939.34, 25% lower, so a wrong window cannot land inside the accepting band.

golden.canonicalQuery: run: t_order_items -> { where: created_at >= @2025-05-25 and created_at <= @2025-09-15; aggregate: summer_sales is sale_price.sum() }

question: How many customers do we have?

golden.rubric: Two answers are defensible and the model resolves neither: 1,000 customers are on file, and 974 have placed at least one order. The model's customer_count measure returns 974, because it counts through the order_items fact table. Match if the answer gives either figure AND says which basis it used. Near match if it gives 974 or 1,000 with no basis stated. No match if it gives any other number, or asserts one figure as the only answer while dismissing the other. Naming both, with the difference explained, is the best answer and a match.
golden.mustState: 974 or 1,000, and which basis it used

verification.primaryAxis: not applicable: a criteria golden holds no value
verification.note: Counted both ways for evidence: 1000 rows in customers, 974 distinct customer_ids in order_items. The 26 who have never ordered are the whole of the difference.
